q: Which of the following is used for window systems made of lightweight, corrosion-resistant material, often used in modern residential and commercial buildings?
n: Figure C is an aluminum window frame section: aluminum is lightweight and corrosion-resistant, so it is the standard frame for modern houses and commercial buildings. Source: AAMA/WDMA/CSA 101/I.S.2/A440; window manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used for windows that open outward from the bottom while hinged at the top, allowing ventilation even during rain?
n: Figure B is a friction stay (projecting hinge), which lets a top-hung window open outward at the bottom and stay open, so it ventilates even in rain. Source: Window hardware manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used for windows that operate by moving panels horizontally along a track for space- saving ventilation?
n: Figure A is the sliding track and roller set that lets sashes move horizontally, venting without swinging into the room. Source: Window hardware manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used as a device to prevent a door or window from opening too far and to absorb the impact when fully open?
n: Figure D is a rubber stopper (stop/buffer) that limits how far a door or window opens and cushions the impact. Source: BHMA A156.16 (auxiliary hardware); manufacturer literature.

q: What is Figure A that is a type of hardware used in frameless glass swing doors to securely connect glass panels and allow for adjustable pivoting at the joints?
n: A patch fitting clamps the corners of a frameless tempered glass door and houses the pivot or connection to the adjacent glass, with adjustable pivoting. Source: Glass door hardware manufacturer literature (Dorma, Geze).

q: Which of the following is a dummy doorknob, typically used for decorative purposes on doors that do not require a latch mechanism?
n: A dummy knob has no latch or spindle. It is a fixed pull used on doors held by ball catches or on the inactive leaf of a pair, so it is decorative and functional only as a handle. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; BHMA A156 hardware terminology.

q: Figure A is a hardware used for:
n: A floor spring (floor closer) is set in a box in the floor under the pivot of a swing door, controlling closing speed and holding the door open. It is common on glass and heavy entrance doors. Source: BHMA A156.4/A156.6 (door controls); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Figure B is a door hardware used for:
n: The pictured hardware is heavy-duty, sized for heavy doors with frequent use, such as institutional or entrance doors. Light closet doors use lighter hinges and catches. Source: BHMA A156 grading of builders' hardware.

q: Figure C is a:
n: A rim lock is surface-mounted on the inside face of the door rather than set into the edge, with its keeper on the jamb. Mortise locks sit in a pocket in the door edge. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; BHMA A156 hardware terminology.

q: Figure D can only be used on a:
n: The light pneumatic (tube) closer shown is made for lightweight screen and storm doors. It is too weak for solid wood or metal doors, which use hydraulic closers. Source: Manufacturer literature for screen door closers; BHMA A156.4.

q: Figure E is a kind of:
n: A mortise lock's body is fitted into a deep pocket (mortise) cut into the door edge. It combines latch and deadbolt and is strong enough for main and commercial doors. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; BHMA A156.13 (mortise locks).

q: Figure 28-C: What is Figure A?
n: In the exploded knob lockset, A is the interior knob, the handle on the room side that turns the spindle to retract the latch. Source: BHMA A156.2 (bored and preassembled locks); manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-C: What is Figure B?
n: B is the shank, the neck of the knob that connects it to the lock chassis and carries the spindle into the door. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-C: What is Figure C?
n: C is the rose, the round plate that covers the bore hole and trims the knob against the door face. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-C: What is Figure D?
n: D is the cylinder lock, the keyed mechanism (pin tumblers) that locks and unlocks the knob from the outside. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-C: What is Figure E?
n: E is the strike plate, the metal plate fixed on the door jamb that receives the latch bolt and protects the wood. Source: BHMA A156.2; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Figure 28-D: What is Figure A?
n: A is the mounting plate, which is screwed to the door face behind the rose and holds the lockset chassis in place. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-D: What is Figure B?
n: B is the cylinder lock body (chassis) that houses the keyed cylinder and drives the latch. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-D: What is Figure C?
n: C is the faceplate, the plate on the door edge through which the latch bolt projects. Source: BHMA A156.2; manufacturer installation diagrams.

q: Figure 28-D: What is Figure D?
n: D is the spring clip that snaps into the slot of the knob shank and holds the knob on the spindle. Source: Manufacturer installation diagrams for knob locksets.

q: What is Figure E?
n: E is the slot in the knob shank. The spring clip engages it to retain the knob, and pressing the clip through the slot releases the knob for removal. Source: Manufacturer installation diagrams for knob locksets.

q: Identify Figure A that is a type of hinge that uses the weight of the door to help it return to the closed position, commonly used on gates and swinging doors.
n: A gravity (rising butt) hinge has helical knuckles that lift the door slightly as it opens, so the door's own weight swings it shut. It is common on gates and toilet doors. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; BHMA A156.1 (butts and hinges).

q: Identify Figure B that is a hinge with a removable central pin, allowing easy detachment of a door without unscrewing the leaf plates.
n: A loose-pin hinge has a pin that can be pulled out, so the door can be lifted off without unscrewing the leaves. Fixed (non-removable) pins are used for security doors. Source: BHMA A156.1; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Identify Figure C that is a continuous hinge that runs the full height or length of the door, offering uniform support and alignment.
n: A piano (continuous) hinge runs the full height of the door, spreading the load along the whole edge for uniform support and alignment. Source: BHMA A156.26 (continuous hinges); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Identify Figure D that is a hinge mounted inside the cabinet body, allowing the door to close flush and remain hidden from view.
n: A concealed (European cup) hinge is set into a bored cup in the cabinet door and mounted inside the carcass, so it is hidden when the door is closed and allows adjustment. Source: Cabinet hardware manufacturer literature (Blum, Hettich); BHMA A156.9.

q: Identify Figure E that is a self-closing hinge with a built-in mechanism that forces the door shut once opened.
n: A spring hinge has a coiled spring inside the barrel that closes the door automatically after opening. It is common on screen doors and fire-rated doors. Source: BHMA A156.17 (self-closing hinges); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is used in frameless glass swing doors, providing pivot support while maintaining a frameless look?
n: The pictured hardware is a patch or pivot fitting for frameless tempered glass doors. It clamps the glass at top and bottom corners and supports the door on pivots, so no frame is needed. Source: Glass door hardware manufacturer literature (Dorma, Geze); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which of the following is used in aluminum swing doors, allowing the door to open and close on side hinges?
n: Figure B is a narrow-backset lockset made for the slim stiles of aluminum swing doors, which are hung on side hinges. Source: Aluminum door hardware manufacturer literature; BHMA A156.

q: Which of the following is used in metal swing doors, allowing the door to open and close securely on strong side hinges?
n: Figure E is a heavy-duty latch lock suited to steel doors, which are hung on strong butt hinges. Source: Steel door hardware literature; BHMA A156.

q: Which of the following is used in aluminum sliding doors, providing smooth horizontal movement of door panels?
n: Figure A is the flush hook lock and roller set for aluminum sliding doors, which slide horizontally on rollers in a track. Source: Aluminum sliding door manufacturer literature.

q: Which of the following is used in frameless glass sliding doors, ensuring sleek and quiet sliding without a visible frame?
n: Figure C is the top-hung roller and clamp hardware for frameless glass sliding doors. It grips the glass and runs quietly in a concealed track. Source: Glass door hardware manufacturer literature (Dorma, Geze).

q: What lock fits two bores at right angles, one through the door face and one through the edge?
n: A cylindrical (bored) lock installs in two holes: a large cross-bore through the door face and a smaller edge bore for the latch. Source: BHMA A156.2 (bored locks); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which type of bolt can be operated from one side only?
n: A barrel bolt is a surface sliding bolt that can only be worked from the side it is mounted on, so it gives privacy or security from the inside. Source: BHMA A156.16 (auxiliary hardware); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What adds a second layer of security to a main door lockset?
n: A deadbolt throws a solid bolt that cannot be pushed back without the key or thumbturn. It adds a second, stronger lock to a main door. Source: BHMA A156.36 (auxiliary locks); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which lockset suits interior doors that need no locking?
n: A passage set latches the door with knobs or levers on both sides but has no lock. It is used for halls and closets. Privacy sets lock from inside and mortise sets lock with a key. Source: BHMA A156.2 lock functions.

q: Which lockset combines a latch and a deadbolt in one unit?
n: A mortise lock fits a single case into the door edge that houses both the spring latch and a deadbolt, often with a key cylinder and thumbturn. Source: BHMA A156.13 (mortise locks); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.
